investigations.name: BASS-II
investigations.full_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II
investigations.description: Conducted inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) aboard the International Space Station, BASS-II examined ignition, flame spread, stabilization, and low-speed forced-flow extinction limits of solid polymers and cotton-fiberglass composite fabrics (SIBAL, PMMA, Nomex) across opposed and concurrent airflows.
investigations.principal_investigators: Sandra L. Olson, Paul V. Ferkul (NASA Glenn Research Center)
investigations.status: Verified Primary Assets + Published PSI/NTRS Test Matrix

investigations.name: FLEX
investigations.description: Investigated liquid fuel droplet combustion (n-heptane, methanol, octane) inside the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus. Mapped radiative and diffusive extinction limits, gaseous suppressant effectiveness, and discovered quasi-steady low-temperature cool flames.
investigations.principal_investigators: Forman A. Williams, Daniel L. Dietrich, Vedha Nayagam (NASA GRC)
investigations.status: Verified PSI-69 Record + NTRS Published Limits

investigations.name: SAFFIRE
investigations.description: Large-scale spacecraft fire growth and combustion product transport experiments conducted inside uncrewed Cygnus resupply vehicles after ISS unberthing. Tested full-scale SIBAL cloth, cotton, PMMA, and Nomex across standard cabin (101 kPa, 21% O2) and exploration (54–71 kPa, 26–31% O2) atmospheres.
investigations.principal_investigators: David L. Urban, Gary A. Ruff, Paul V. Ferkul (NASA GRC)

investigations.name: SPICE
investigations.description: Measured laminar smoke points, flame lengths, and soot inception thresholds of non-buoyant gas-jet diffusion flames (ethylene, methane, propane) in co-flowing oxidizer streams aboard the ISS to isolate chemistry and diffusive transport without buoyancy distortion.
investigations.principal_investigators: David L. Urban, Peter B. Sunderland, Jerry Ku (NASA GRC)
investigations.status: Verified PSI-60 Record + NTRS Smoke-Point Data

investigations.name: SAME-R
investigations.description: Quantified size distributions and particle morphology of oxidative pyrolysis smoke generated by overheating five representative spacecraft materials (lamp wick, Kapton, Teflon, silicone rubber, Pyrell foam) below ignition to improve spacecraft smoke detector discrimination and reduce false alarms.
investigations.principal_investigators: David L. Urban (NASA GRC), George W. Mulholland (NIST)
investigations.status: Verified PSI-101 Record + TEM Particle Distributions

findings.title: Low-Speed Forced Airflow Sustains Dim-Blue Flames Below 1g Flammability Limits
findings.researchers: Sandra L. Olson, Paul V. Ferkul (NASA Glenn Research Center)
findings.scientific_objective: Determine whether solid polymers and thin composite fabrics can sustain combustion in microgravity at oxygen concentrations and airflow speeds where normal-gravity (1g) buoyancy tests predict self-extinction.
findings.experimental_conditions: PMMA sheets/rods and SIBAL (75% cotton / 25% fiberglass) tested in ISS MSG wind tunnel across 0–53 cm/s forced flow and 13%–21% O2 at ~101.3 kPa.
findings.observation: In the absence of buoyant convection (~30 cm/s equivalent in 1g), forced flows between 1 and 10 cm/s produced compact, dim-blue flames with minimal soot. When airflow was commanded to zero (as directly observed in BASS_GMT50_SAMPLE_147_TEST_B1 at 10:10:06), flames radiatively quenched within 7 seconds.
findings.important_measurements: SIBAL sustained flame spread down to ~13.5–16% O2 at 3–5 cm/s in 0g, whereas 1g downward spread extinguished at 16% O2. PMMA sustained spread at 2 cm/s in 21% O2 but radiatively extinguished near 0.5 cm/s and blew off near 45 cm/s.
findings.researcher_conclusion: Microgravity exhibits a dual extinction boundary (radiative quenching at ultra-low flow and convective blow-off at high flow). Consequently, standard 1g upward/downward flammability tests (NASA-STD-6001) can under-predict fire persistence in low-ventilation spacecraft environments.
findings.ai_interpretation: FlameGuard synthesis: Spacecraft cabin HVAC dead-zones (< 5 cm/s) present a deceptive hazard—flames may burn dimly with low optical signature, then flare rapidly if ventilation restarts before thermal quenching completes.
findings.safety_implication: Emergency spacecraft fire response protocols that immediately shut down cabin ventilation ('Fan to zero') exploit the radiative extinction floor, provided crew do not prematurely restore airflow while surfaces remain above pyrolysis temperature.
findings.limitations: MSG wind tunnel cross-section restricts maximum sample dimensions; ProofSheet PDFs lack continuous gas-analyzer O2 readings without joining PSI CSV telemetry.
findings.citation: Olson, S. L., & Ferkul, P. V. (2017). Microgravity flammability boundary for solid fuels. Proc. Combust. Inst., 36(2); NASA/TM-20210011385.

findings.title: Two-Stage Droplet Combustion and Persistent Low-Temperature Cool Flames
findings.researchers: Forman A. Williams, Vedha Nayagam, Daniel L. Dietrich (NASA GRC / UC San Diego)
findings.scientific_objective: Characterize liquid fuel droplet burning rates, gaseous fire-suppressant thresholds, and radiative versus diffusive extinction mechanisms without buoyant distortion.
findings.experimental_conditions: n-Heptane and Methanol droplets (D0 = 1.5–4.5 mm) suspended in quiescent CIR/MDCA chambers across 0.7–3.0 atm and 10%–40% O2 diluted with N2, CO2, or He.
findings.observation: Large n-heptane droplets (> 2.5 mm) underwent visible hot-flame radiative extinction yet continued evaporating at a steady rate for tens of seconds, accompanied by OH* chemiluminescence and low-temperature formaldehyde chemistry.
findings.important_measurements: Baseline 1 atm Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI): ~15% O2 for n-heptane and ~12% O2 for methanol. Radiative extinction diameter increased with droplet size, while diffusive extinction diameter increased as O2 decreased.
findings.researcher_conclusion: After high-temperature flame extinction, large alkane droplets can transition into a stable quasi-steady cool flame governed by low-temperature peroxy-radical kinetics (~500–800 K), releasing heat invisibly without visible soot luminescence.
findings.ai_interpretation: FlameGuard synthesis: Visible flame extinction does not guarantee reaction termination for hydrocarbon fuels in microgravity; optical flame sensors alone may miss persistent cool-flame vapor generation.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft fire-suppression validation must verify complete chemical quenching (via temperature and CO/CH2O gas sensors) rather than relying solely on visible-light optical extinction.
findings.limitations: Quiescent droplet suspension does not capture forced ventilation convective effects; cool-flame persistence strongly depends on alkane chain length and chamber pressure.
findings.citation: Nayagam, V., Dietrich, D. L., Ferkul, P. V., Hicks, M. C., & Williams, F. A. (2012). Can cool flames support quasi-steady alkane droplet burning? Combust. Flame; PSI-69.

findings.title: Large-Scale Fire Growth & Elevated Oxygen Risk in Hypobaric Exploration Atmospheres
findings.researchers: David L. Urban, Gary A. Ruff, Paul V. Ferkul (NASA GRC)
findings.topic: Large-Scale Spacecraft Fire Growth & Exploration Atmospheres
findings.scientific_objective: Bridge small-scale ISS glovebox results (BASS-II) to realistic spacecraft module scales and evaluate flammability in future Artemis/Gateway exploration atmospheres.
findings.experimental_conditions: Six uncrewed Cygnus flight campaigns (Saffire I–VI): 101 kPa / 21% O2 (Saffire I–III), 100 kPa / 22% O2 (IV), 71 kPa / 26.2–31% O2 (V), and 54.5 kPa / 28.8–30.3% O2 (VI) with 5–30 cm/s duct airflow.
findings.observation: Large SIBAL samples achieved steady flame spread across the full 0.4 m width; increasing flow from 20 cm/s (Saffire-I) to 30 cm/s (Saffire-III) substantially accelerated spread rate and flame length. Elevated O2 in hypobaric 54–71 kPa exploration atmospheres markedly increased ignition propensity.
findings.important_measurements: SIBAL concurrent spread accelerated from ~0.80 cm/s at 20 cm/s flow (Saffire-I) to ~1.25 cm/s at 30 cm/s flow (Saffire-III). Saffire-V/VI confirmed rapid burning at 26.2%–31.0% O2 despite lower total pressure (54.5–71 kPa).
findings.researcher_conclusion: Small-scale tests capture qualitative trends, but full-scale spacecraft fires exhibit stronger radiative feedback and multi-zone smoke/CO transport dynamics that must be modeled at vehicle scale.
findings.ai_interpretation: FlameGuard synthesis: Exploration habitats operating at 55–71 kPa with 28–30% O2 (to maintain normoxic partial pressure for crew) face higher flame-spread sensitivity than ISS 101 kPa / 21% O2 baselines.
findings.safety_implication: Future lunar Gateway and Mars transit habitats require stricter material-selection margins and rapid multi-sensor CO/smoke detection tuned for enriched O2 hypobaric cabins.
findings.limitations: Uncrewed Cygnus post-departure test window limits total burn iterations per flight; Saffire-VI detailed telemetry reduction remains ongoing (NTRS 20240007488).
findings.citation: Urban, D. L., Ferkul, P., Olson, S., et al. (2020). Fire Safety Journal, 118, 102977; NTRS 20240007488.

findings.title: Non-Buoyant Gas-Jet Flames Produce Longer Luminous Zones and Earlier Soot Inception
findings.researchers: David L. Urban, Peter B. Sunderland, Jerry Ku (NASA GRC / Univ. of Maryland)
findings.scientific_objective: Determine laminar smoke points and flame shapes of hydrocarbon gas jets in microgravity to separate chemical sooting propensity from buoyant acceleration.
findings.experimental_conditions: Ethylene (C2H4), Methane (CH4), and Propane co-flowing laminar jet flames in air (~21% O2, 101.3 kPa, 15–18 cm/s co-flow) compared directly against 1g controls.
findings.observation: Removing buoyancy lengthened residence time inside the fuel-rich core, producing wider, ~50% longer ethylene flames in microgravity (6.4 cm in 0g vs 4.1 cm in 1g) and shifting soot inception to lower fuel flow rates.
findings.important_measurements: Ethylene flame length increased from 4.1 cm (1g) to 6.4 cm (0g) under matched flow rates, with enhanced radiative cooling from trapped soot.
findings.researcher_conclusion: Buoyancy on Earth accelerates hot gases out of the reaction zone, artificially suppressing soot residence time; microgravity laminar smoke points are fundamentally lower for sooting hydrocarbons.
findings.ai_interpretation: FlameGuard synthesis: Microgravity hydrocarbon leaks produce larger soot volumes per unit fuel mass, increasing radiative heat transfer to adjacent wiring harnesses while altering optical smoke signatures.
findings.safety_implication: CFD fire models calibrated on 1g jet flames will underpredict flame length and soot radiation in spacecraft unless buoyancy terms are decoupled.
findings.limitations: Laminar co-flow nozzle geometry represents small pressurized leaks rather than turbulent high-momentum ruptures.
findings.citation: Urban, D. L., Sunderland, P. B., & Ku, J. Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets, NASA PSI-60.

findings.title: Microgravity Pyrolysis Smoke Particles Cluster in 200–400 nm Range, Challenging Optical Detectors
findings.researchers: David L. Urban (NASA GRC), George W. Mulholland (NIST)
findings.scientific_objective: Measure smoke aerosol particle size distributions from overheated spacecraft materials in microgravity to optimize ISS and exploration smoke detector sensitivity.
findings.experimental_conditions: Five spacecraft materials (cotton lamp wick, Kapton, Teflon, silicone rubber, Pyrell foam) heated in MSG airflow and quiescent aging chambers; TEM grids + ionization/obscuration diagnostics.
findings.observation: Smoke particulates generated under low-gravity oxidative pyrolysis consistently centered between 200 nm and 400 nm, with quiescent aging fostering larger fractal/chain-like agglomerates.
findings.important_measurements: Mean aerosol diameters: Lamp wick ~210 nm, Kapton ~240 nm, Teflon ~270 nm, Pyrell foam ~310 nm, Silicone rubber ~350 nm.
findings.researcher_conclusion: Because microgravity smoke plumes do not rise buoyantly to ceiling sensors and exhibit distinct sub-micron particle distributions (200–400 nm), spacecraft detectors tuned only for terrestrial ~1 µm nuisance dust or flaming soot suffer delayed response or false alarms.
findings.ai_interpretation: FlameGuard synthesis: Dual-wavelength optical scattering paired with CO/gas sensing is necessary to distinguish sub-300 nm Kapton/Teflon overheating aerosols from cabin dust.
findings.safety_implication: Directly informs next-generation spacecraft smoke detector calibration (such as ISS and Orion optical-scattering & ionization threshold curves).
findings.limitations: TEM grid sampling captures discrete aging snapshots rather than continuous real-time coagulation kinetics across an entire cabin.
findings.citation: Urban, D. L., Mulholland, G. W., et al. Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight (SAME-R), NASA PSI-101.
